title: Best Microwaves of 2026: 9 Countertop Microwave Ovens Reviewed
excerpt: Nine countertop microwaves compared, from compact 0.7-cubic-foot models to the full-size Toshiba with a smart sensor: who each suits, and how to choose size and wattage.
html:
A good microwave is the most used appliance in many kitchens: it reheats leftovers, steams vegetables, softens butter and makes popcorn in minutes. The differences between models come down to a few things: size, wattage, whether it has a sensor, and how easy it is to use and clean.

This guide compares nine countertop microwaves, from compact 0.7-cubic-foot models for dorms and offices to full-size 1.2-cubic-foot ovens for families: the Toshiba EM131A5C-BS, two BLACK+DECKER models, two Farberware models, two Chefman models, the Commercial Chef and the Nostalgia Retro. For each one you will find who it suits, its strengths and limits, and a buying guide to help you pick the right size and power.

How We Chose These Microwaves

1

Size for the household

Whether a dinner plate fits, and how much counter space the cabinet takes.

2

Power

At least 900 to 1,000 watts for a main microwave; 700 watts only where a compact size matters more.

3

Ease of use

Clear controls, useful one-touch presets and features such as a sensor, ECO mode or mute.

4

Safety and cleaning

Child locks, a removable turntable and an interior that wipes clean.

5

Brand and support

Established brands with widely available service and parts.

Detailed Reviews: The 9 Best Countertop Microwaves

1
Best Overall

Toshiba EM131A5C-BS Countertop Microwave

Best for: Most kitchens: a full-size countertop microwave that reheats and cooks evenly with little guesswork.

Check price on Amazon

The Toshiba EM131A5C-BS is the microwave to beat for most homes. Its 1.2 cubic feet and 12.4-inch turntable fit a full dinner plate or a casserole dish, and the smart humidity sensor reads the steam coming off the food to adjust cooking time and power, so reheated leftovers are less likely to come out dry or cold in the middle.

There are 12 auto menus for common foods, an ECO mode that cuts standby power, and a mute button for anyone tired of the beeps. Amazon lists it at 1,000 watts; some versions of the listing say 1,100 W, so check the page you buy from.

It is a countertop model: Toshiba does not recommend building it in or installing it over a range.

Pros

  • Smart humidity sensor
  • Fits a full dinner plate (12.4-inch turntable)
  • 12 auto menus
  • ECO mode and mute button
  • Black stainless finish

Cons

  • Countertop only, not for built-in use
  • Wattage differs between listing versions
  • Larger footprint than compact models

Verdict: The best all-round microwave for most kitchens, thanks to the sensor and the full-size turntable.

Microwave Buying Guide: How to Choose

1. Size: what fits inside

CapacityGood for
0.7 cu ftDorms, offices, RVs: mugs, bowls, small plates
0.9 cu ftApartments and couples: most dinner plates
1.1 to 1.2 cu ftFamilies: full dinner plates and casserole dishes
1.5 cu ft and upLarge households and big dishes

Check the turntable diameter if you use large plates, and measure your counter space, leaving room at the sides and back for ventilation as the manual specifies.

2. Wattage: how fast it heats

Higher wattage heats faster and more evenly. Most packaged-food directions assume about 1,000 to 1,100 watts, so a 700-watt microwave needs extra time. For a main kitchen microwave, choose 900 watts or more.

3. Sensor cooking and inverter technology

A humidity sensor, like the Toshiba’s, adjusts time and power from the steam the food releases, which makes reheating and popcorn more reliable. Inverter microwaves deliver steady low power instead of switching on and off, which helps defrosting; none of our picks use an inverter, which keeps their prices down.

4. Type: countertop, over-the-range or built-in

Countertop microwaves, like all nine here, are the cheapest and need no installation. Over-the-range models replace a range hood and vent the cooktop; built-in models need a trim kit made for that model. Never build in a countertop microwave unless the maker allows it, because it needs space to vent.

5. Controls and safety

One-touch presets save time for popcorn, potatoes and drinks. A child lock matters in family kitchens, and a mute button is welcome in apartments and shared spaces.

6. Power outlet

Plug a microwave straight into a grounded wall outlet, ideally on a circuit it doesn’t share with a kettle or toaster, and avoid extension cords; the manual gives the exact requirements.

Using and Caring for Your Microwave

  • Use microwave-safe glass or ceramic, and read can you microwave Styrofoam before reheating takeout.
  • Cover food loosely and stir halfway for even heating.
  • Clean spills while they are fresh; our guide to cleaning a microwave with lemon, vinegar and steam shows how.
  • Try quick recipes like steamed broccoli or a poached egg in one minute, and defrost safely with our chicken defrosting guide.

Microwave FAQ

Is a 700-watt microwave powerful enough?

For reheating drinks, leftovers and small portions, yes, but it is slower. Add time to package directions written for 1,000 watts or more. For a main family microwave, 900 to 1,000 watts or more is better.

What size microwave should I buy?

About 0.7 cubic feet for a dorm or office, 0.9 for one or two people, and 1.1 to 1.2 for a family or for full dinner plates.

Is a sensor microwave worth it?

If you reheat a lot, yes: the sensor adjusts the time from the steam the food releases, so you guess less. For simple tasks, presets and a timer work fine.

How long do microwaves last?

Many last around seven to ten years with normal use. Keeping the inside clean and never running it empty helps.

Can I put a countertop microwave in a cabinet?

Only if the manual allows it, usually with a trim kit made for that model. Otherwise it can overheat without space to vent.

How do microwaves work?

They use microwaves to make water molecules in food vibrate and heat up. Our how microwaves work explainer goes into detail, and are microwaves bad for you? covers safety.

Are microwaves safe?

Yes, when used as the manufacturer directs and the door seals properly. Use microwave-safe containers and don’t run a microwave with a damaged door.
